Antics

AN-tiks -- almost always used in the plural, as in 'silly antics.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Antics is foolish, outlandish, or amusing behavior, especially playful mischief.

The puppy's silly antics during the wedding video became an internet sensation.

Worked Example

A group of toddlers at a birthday party start wearing their paper hats upside down, chasing balloons across the yard, and giggling uncontrollably at nothing in particular.

That playful, silly, slightly chaotic behavior is exactly what antics describes. Unlike 'manners,' which implies polite, controlled conduct, antics are lighthearted and a little wild.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hijinks: Hijinks is boisterous, high-spirited fun -- loud, rowdy, and usually shared by a whole group. Antics is broader and quieter: any pattern of silly or playful behavior, noisy or not, from a single pet or child as easily as from a rowdy group.

tomfoolery: Tomfoolery is silly, foolish carrying-on done purely for laughs, and the word carries a mild scolding, as if the fun is a waste of time. Antics simply names the playful or mischievous behavior itself, without any built-in disapproval from the speaker.

horseplay: Horseplay is rough, physical play between people -- shoving, wrestling, chasing -- the kind that can end with something broken. Antics covers playful or mischievous behavior of any sort, physical or not, and does not suggest anyone is being knocked around.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

decorum: behavior that is polite and in good taste

solemnity: the state of being serious and dignified

Where it sits · how lasting and tricky the silliness is — capers → antics → shenanigans

capers vs. antics: Capers can feel a bit lighter than antics -- capers often describes brief, playful escapades, while antics can describe an ongoing pattern of silly or mischievous behavior.

shenanigans vs. antics: Shenanigans can feel more mischievous than antics: antics is often simply silly or amusing, while shenanigans can carry a stronger hint of trickery or minor rule-breaking.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -antiqu-

root — -antiqu-: ancient, old (Italian antico, from Latin antiquus)

Put it together

Put it together: Antics traces back to Italian antico, 'ancient,' used in the Renaissance to describe strange, grotesque figures carved in an old-fashioned style. Over time, 'antic' shifted from describing odd ancient decorations to describing odd, playful behavior -- the same root that gives us antique.

Use the root in a new word: antique

Use the root in a new word: antique: The collector proudly displayed a two-hundred-year-old antique clock on the mantel.
